name: Archimedes' mechanical method for areas and volumes
why: Balancing figures on a lever (centres of gravity) is used to discover area and volume results later proved by exhaustion.

institutional.basis: no naming, textbook or institution found

took.label: Mechanical discovery of the parabola's area

phases: Lever law and centres of gravity

ms.l: Democritus asserts the cone and pyramid volumes
ms.d: Democritus first stated that cone and pyramid are one third of cylinder and prism, a result Archimedes says he discovered by his method.
ms.n: Dated by Democritus' working life; the argument is a reconstruction.

ev.c: Democritus was first to assert these volumes; Eudoxus first proved them.
ev.s: Heath, The Method of Archimedes (1912), introduction

ms.l: Quadrature of the Parabola outlines the mechanical method
ms.w: Archimedes, Quadrature of the Parabola (letter to Dositheus)
ms.d: Archimedes gives the area of a parabolic segment first by a lever argument and then by exhaustion.
ms.n: Archimedes lived 287-212 BC and his works are undated, so the range is an outer bound. This work is also the first_application below.

ev.c: He first outlines the mechanical proof in Quadrature of the Parabola next to the geometric one, and gives a fuller account in The Method.
Heath's order places the Parabola before the Method.
The Quadrature of the Parabola gives two proofs of the main theorem: one by abstract mechanics (a lever in equilibrium) and one by pure geometry

ms.l: Mechanical discovery of the parabola's area
ms.w: Archimedes, Quadrature of the Parabola
ms.d: The lever argument is used to find the area of a parabolic segment, later confirmed by exhaustion.
ms.n: Same work as the first_statement, listed twice because it carries both the statement and the first use.

ev.c: Same source as above: the mechanical argument appears alongside the geometric proof.
Same lever argument in the Quadrature of the Parabola

ms.w: Archimedes, Method concerning mechanical theorems, letter to Eratosthenes
ms.d: Archimedes explains in a letter how balancing slices of figures led him to results such as sphere and cylinder volumes, which he then proved by exhaustion.
ms.n: MacTutor follows Heath's order, which places the Method immediately before On the Sphere and Cylinder, hence after the Quadrature of the Parabola; all dates remain the outer bound of Archimedes's life.

ev.c: It is a letter to Eratosthenes and holds the first attested explicit use of indivisibles.
ev.s: Wikipedia, The Method of Mechanical Theorems

ev.c: Archimedes states that some results became clear by a mechanical method before geometric proof.

ms.n: Crossref has no record of Heiberg's 1907 Hermes article; Wikipedia says Heiberg photographed the palimpsest in 1906 and published the text between 1910 and 1915. The milestone is the 1906 discovery.

ev.c: In the summer of 1906 Heiberg discovered the manuscript that includes The Method.
The work was thought lost until its rediscovery in the palimpsest in 1906.

notes: Direct-style review in progress (not promoted). Re-read MacTutor (Heath's order of the works; summer 1906 discovery) and Wikipedia (Quadrature of the Parabola: mechanical and geometric proofs side by side; Archimedes Palimpsest: photographed 1906, published 1910-15). name: Probability from games of chance
why: The problem of points and dice questions are solved by counting equally likely cases, then generalised into a calculus of chance and, with Laplace, an analytic one.

methodological.basis: earliest key development; no first application found

took.label: Ars conjectandi and the law of large numbers

phases: Counting for the problem of points (Pascal and Fermat, 1654)

ms.w: Luca Pacioli, Summa de arithmetica, geometrica, proportioni et proportionalita, 1494
ms.d: Early printed treatment of the interrupted game that divided the stake by rounds already won, a rule Tartaglia later criticised; neither used counting of future outcomes.
ms.ph: Counting for the problem of points (Pascal and Fermat, 1654)

ev.c: Pacioli treated the interrupted game in 1494 by proportion to rounds won; Tartaglia found the rule defective.

ms.n: The 1663 printing date is stated in secondary literature; I only located a 1961 English edition record on archive.org (bookongamesofcha00card), so the printing year is not independently confirmed.

ev.c: Cardano's dice work dates from the 1560s and was not published until around 100 years later.

ms.l: Pascal-Fermat correspondence solves the problem of points by counting equally likely futures

ev.c: Their correspondence of summer 1654 treated the dice problem and the problem of points.
Fermat's method counted the equally likely continuations; Pascal gave a step-by-step recursion and a binomial formula.

name: Pingala: combinatorics of poetic metres

ms.n: Wikipedia's Virahanka page dates Pingala to the 4th century BCE, his own page to the 3rd or 2nd; the range follows the latter. Claims of binary notation and an early zero are modern interpretations.

ev.c: He was an Indian prosodist, 6th to 8th century, building on Pingala, regarded as first to propose the Fibonacci sequence.

ms.n: Both the explicit triangle and its Sanskrit name appear here; one milestone covers both.

ev.c: His method of pyramidal expansion (meru-prastara) is equivalent to Pascal's triangle; he lived in the 10th century.

name: Babylonian astronomical parameters enter Greek astronomy
why: Greek geometric lunar models were tested and calibrated against Babylonian period parameters and eclipse records.

ev.c: He was the first to divide the zodiac into 360 degrees and used arithmetic progressions.
The division was probably introduced for all circles by Hypsicles, in Hipparchus' time.

ev.c: For his lunar theory he needed mean motions and the best data were Babylonian parameters (Toomer quoted).

name: Pythagorean number theory and musical ratios
why: Whole-number ratios behind consonant string lengths supported a programme of studying even, odd, triangular and perfect numbers as objects in themselves.

methodological.basis: earliest key development; no first application found

ms.l: Tradition credits Pythagoras with the concord ratios
ms.d: Later tradition makes Pythagoras the discoverer that octave, fifth and fourth match 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3, though the evidence is indirect.
ms.n: Attribution to Pythagoras himself is disputed; sources are late. Dated by his floruit, not by any text.

ev.c: MacTutor says Pythagoras noticed that string lengths in whole-number ratios give harmonious tones.
The correspondence is reflected in early Pythagorean sayings and so was probably known to Pythagoras, but the famous workshop story would not work.
The same entry doubts that Pythagoras himself was a mathematician or worked out the detailed mathematics.

ms.l: Philolaus builds the cosmos on the concord ratios
ms.w: Philolaus, fragments (esp. Fr. 6a), late 5th c. BC
ms.d: The earliest surviving Pythagorean text to use the octave, fifth and fourth ratios as a structural principle is Philolaus' book, known only from fragments.
ms.n: Fragments are quoted by later authors, so the book has no publication year; the range is Philolaus' working life. Hippasus (experiment with bronze discs, reported by Aristoxenus) may be earlier; see notes.

ev.c: Philolaus' conception of the cosmos centred on the match between the three concords and the ratios 2:1, 3:2, 4:3.
Philolaus, born about 470, taught the preceding generation of Pythagoreans before Archytas.
Standard modern study and edition of the fragments.
ev.s: Huffman, Philolaus of Croton (Cambridge University Press, 1993)

ms.l: Archytas: ratio theory and the four sciences
ms.w: Archytas, Fr. 1 and testimonia (DK 47)

ev.c: He proved that superparticular ratios (n+1):n cannot be split by a mean proportional, and Fr. 1 is the earliest text naming the four sciences.
Standard modern edition and commentary.
ev.s: Huffman, Archytas of Tarentum (Cambridge University Press, 2005)

ms.w: Euclid, Elements, Books VII-IX (IX.36), c. 300 BC
ms.d: Euclid defines perfect numbers in Book VII and proves in IX.36 that 2^(k-1)(2^k-1) is perfect when 2^k-1 is prime, turning Pythagorean number lore into a theorem.
ms.n: Euclid's date is inferred (c. 300 BC).

ev.c: The first known result on perfect numbers is Elements IX.36.
Definition VII.22 names perfect numbers and IX.36 gives the formation rule.
Primary text of IX.36 in translation.
ev.s: D. E. Joyce, Euclid's Elements IX.36

ms.w: Nicomachus of Gerasa, Introduction to Arithmetic, c. 100 AD
ms.d: Nicomachus gives the first stand-alone Pythagorean arithmetic: classes of numbers (perfect, abundant, deficient), figurate numbers and the link to musical ratios, stated without proofs.
ms.n: MacTutor puts his life at about 60 to 120; the work is dated only by his floruit.

ev.c: It was the first work to treat arithmetic apart from geometry and stayed the standard text for centuries.
Nicomachus classified numbers by perfect, superabundant and deficient, writing around 100 AD.
English translation by D'Ooge (1926).
ev.s: Nicomachus, Introduction to Arithmetic (Open Library record)

ms.d: Wikipedia reports that the fifth-based tuning later called Pythagorean already existed in ancient Mesopotamia, so musical ratios were probably used before the Greek theory.
ms.n: Wikipedia gives no dated tablet; searched Wikipedia and MacTutor only. Keep as an open lead, not a ranked date.

ev.c: Pythagorean tuning is said to date back to ancient Mesopotamia and was misattributed to Pythagoras.
